title: Extended Topic: The Four Basic Forces—An Introduction
lead: Only four distinct forces account for every known phenomenon, and nearly everything you feel directly is one of them. This section names the gravitational, the electromagnetic, the weak nuclear and the strong nuclear force and sets their strengths, ranges and carrier particles side by side, and then asks how a force reaches across a distance at all, first through the field that surrounds whatever creates it and then through the particles that field exchanges.
objectives: Understand the four basic forces that underlie the processes in nature.
summary_html:
• The various types of forces that are categorized for use in many applications are all manifestations of the four basic forces in nature.
  • The properties of these forces are summarized in Table 4.1.
  • Everything we experience directly without sensitive instruments is due to either electromagnetic forces or gravitational forces. The nuclear forces are responsible for the submicroscopic structure of matter, but they are not directly sensed because of their short ranges. Attempts are being made to show all four forces are different manifestations of a single unified force.
  • A force field surrounds an object creating a force and is the carrier of that force.

figures.original_caption: The electric force field between a positively charged particle and a negatively charged particle. When a positive test charge is placed in the field, the charge will experience a force in the direction of the force field lines.

The exchange of masses resulting in repulsive forces. (a) The person throwing the basketball exerts a force Fp1 on it toward the other person and feels a reaction force FB away from the second person. (b) The person catching the basketball exerts a force Fp2 on it to stop the ball and feels a reaction force F′B away from the first person. (c) The analogous exchange of a meson between a proton and a neutron carries the strong nuclear forces Fexch and F′exch between them. An attractive force can also be exerted by the exchange of a mass—if person 2 pulled the basketball away from the first person as he tried to retain it, then the force between them would be attractive.

exercises.prompt: Which phenomenon correctly describes the direction and magnitude of normal forces?

answer.hint: The section says that every class of force we experience directly, except gravity, is due to electromagnetic interactions of atoms and molecules. Ask yourself which way the surface pushes the object that presses into it.

exercises.prompt: Explain which of the four fundamental forces is responsible for a ball bouncing off the ground after it hits, and why this force has this effect.

answer.solution: The ball bounces because of the electromagnetic force. The ball and the ground are both made of atoms, and when the two are pressed together the electrons of one are brought very close to the electrons of the other; like charges repel, and that repulsion is an electromagnetic force. The section says that friction, tension, and all of the other classes of forces we experience directly, except gravity, are due to electromagnetic interactions of atoms and molecules, and the force the ground returns to the ball is one of them. The repulsion grows as the ball presses further into the surface, so it first slows the ball, then stops it, and then drives it back up away from the ground.

exercises.prompt: Which of the basic forces best explains tension in a rope being pulled between two people? Is the acting force causing attraction or repulsion in this instance?

answer.hint: The nuclear forces act only over the size of a nucleus or less, so they cannot reach along a rope. Ask which of the two that remain holds the fibres of the rope to one another, and which way it pulls on the hands at either end.

exercises.prompt: Explain how interatomic electric forces produce the normal force, and why it has the direction it does.

answer.solution: The atoms of a surface are held in place by electric forces, and the atoms of the object resting on it carry charges of their own. Pressing the two together brings like charges close, and like charges repel, so each atom of the surface pushes back on the atom above it; adding those repulsions over the whole area of contact gives the normal force. The object presses into the surface along the line perpendicular to it, which is the line along which the atoms are driven together, so the repulsion they return points along that same line and away from the surface. That is why the normal force is perpendicular to the surface and directed outward from it. Note that the atoms need not actually meet for this to work, as the section says of friction, which is an electromagnetic force between atoms that may not actually touch.

exercises.prompt: The gravitational force is the weakest of the four basic forces. In which case can the electromagnetic, strong, and weak forces be ignored because the gravitational force is so strongly dominant?

options: a person jumping on a trampoline
a rocket blasting off from Earth
a log rolling down a hill

exercises.prompt: Describe a situation in which gravitational force is the dominant force. Why can the other three basic forces be ignored in the situation you described?

answer.solution: The motion of the Moon about Earth is one such situation. The section says that on the very large scale, as in astronomical systems, the gravitational force is the dominant force determining the motions of moons, planets, stars, and galaxies. The weak and the strong nuclear force act over an extremely short range, the size of a nucleus or less, so they do not reach from the one body to the other at all. The electromagnetic force is long range and far stronger than gravity, but a body of that size carries very nearly as much positive charge as negative, so its electromagnetic forces nearly cancel. Gravity is attractive only, so every part of one body pulls on every part of the other and nothing cancels. What is left is gravity.

exercises.prompt: Explain, in terms of the properties of the four basic forces, why people notice the gravitational force acting on their bodies if it is such a comparatively weak force.

answer.solution: Gravity is by far the weakest of the four basic forces, some thirty-six powers of ten below the electromagnetic force, but it is the only one of them that is always attractive. The weak and the strong nuclear force act only over the size of a nucleus or less, so they are never felt outside matter itself. The electromagnetic force can be attractive or repulsive, and a body as large as a person carries so nearly equal amounts of positive and negative charge that its electromagnetic forces nearly cancel. Nothing cancels gravity. Our weight is the gravitational force due to the entire Earth acting on us, and the whole of that mass pulls the one way, so a very weak force with a very large mass behind it and nothing to oppose it is a force we feel all day.

exercises.prompt: What is the dominant force between astronomical objects? Why are the other three basic forces less significant over these very large distances?

answer.solution: Gravity is the dominant force between astronomical objects. The section says that on the very large scale the gravitational force determines the motions of moons, planets, stars, and galaxies. The weak and the strong nuclear force act over an extremely short range, the size of a nucleus or less, so across astronomical distances they do not act at all. The electromagnetic force is long range and much the stronger of the two that are left, but it is attractive and repulsive both, and it nearly cancels for macroscopic objects, which carry very nearly equal positive and negative charge. Gravity is attractive only and never cancels, so it adds over every part of both bodies, and it is what remains at that scale.

exercises.prompt: Give a detailed example of how the exchange of a particle can result in an attractive force. (For example, consider one child pulling a toy out of the hands of another.)

answer.solution: Take the two people of Figure 4.25, but let the second one take the ball rather than be given it. The first person holds the basketball out and tries to keep hold of it, and the second reaches across and pulls it away. In drawing the ball toward themselves the second person is drawn toward the first, since the ball is being taken from that side, and the first person, holding on as the ball goes, is drawn toward the second. Each has been moved toward the other and neither has touched the other, so the exchange of the ball has given an attractive force. The caption of Figure 4.25 makes the same point: if person 2 pulled the basketball away from the first person as he tried to retain it, then the force between them would be attractive. The carrier particles of Table 4.1 do the same thing for the basic forces, which is why an exchange can give the attraction of gravity as well as the repulsion of two like charges.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the strength of the weak nuclear force relative to the strong nuclear force? (b) What is the strength of the weak nuclear force relative to the electromagnetic force? Since the weak nuclear force acts at only very short distances, such as inside nuclei, where the strong and electromagnetic forces also act, it might seem surprising that we have any knowledge of it at all. We have such knowledge because the weak nuclear force is responsible for beta decay, a type of nuclear decay not explained by other forces.

parts.hint: Divide the strength of the weak nuclear force by the strength of the strong nuclear force, which Table 4.1 gives as 1.
Divide the strength of the weak nuclear force by the strength of the electromagnetic force, and subtract the exponents.

exercises.prompt: What is the ratio of the strength of the strong nuclear force to that of the electromagnetic force? Based on this ratio, you might expect that the strong force dominates the nucleus, which is true for small nuclei. Large nuclei, however, have sizes greater than the range of the strong nuclear force. At these sizes, the electromagnetic force begins to affect nuclear stability. These facts will be used to explain nuclear fusion and fission later in this text.

answer.hint: Take the strong nuclear force’s strength of 1 over the electromagnetic force’s $10^{-2}$, which is the two rungs the ladder in the text brackets by default.
